notes.meaning: David turns away from earthly helps and idols to offer his whole heart to the Lord. Lifting up the soul means setting one's love and desires entirely upon God. It is handing over one's life into God's hands as a sacred trust in honest prayer.

David places his full reliance on God and asks not to suffer bitter disappointment. To be put to shame means to have one's hope fail and become an object of ridicule. He asks God to protect him so his enemies cannot celebrate his downfall.

David widens his prayer to include all believers who wait on the Lord with patient hope. None who look to God in faithful expectation will ever be let down. True disgrace belongs only to those who act treacherously and break faith without any cause.

David asks God to show him how to live and teach him the right path to take. People are often blind to God's will and need divine instruction to understand their duty. Asking for God's path means wanting to obey His commands through every hard test.

David pleads to be led into God's truth as revealed in His Word. Since God is the one who rescues him, David spends his entire day waiting in quiet trust for divine direction. Patient trust gives believers courage when they face uncertainty.

David calls on God to act according to His ancient character of tender mercy and deep, loyal love. These compassions are not new, for God has shown them to His people from ages past. He asks God to remember that same eternal kindness toward him right now.

David confesses the thoughtless sins of his youth as well as his later deliberate rebellions against God. He asks the Lord not to hold those past failures against him. His plea rests entirely on God's free goodness and mercy, not on any merit of his own.

God is naturally good and perfectly upright in all His ways. Because He is good, He does not immediately destroy wayward people, but calls sinners to repentance, which means turning away from sin. His holiness and kindness work together to show them the path to life.

God guides those who are humble and contrite over their sins. Proud people think they know best, but those who admit their weakness are ready to be taught. God gently directs such teachable souls to make choices that are pleasing to Him.

Every path God takes in leading His people is marked by loving devotion and reliable truth. Even painful trials work for the good of those who keep His covenant, which is His sacred promise of relationship and rules for life. Believers who cling to God's Word find that His promises never fail.

David asks for the pardon of his iniquity, which means his great guilt and moral failure, for the honor of God's name alone. He presents the very heaviness of his sin as a reason to seek mercy, knowing only a great Savior can heal so deep a wound. When God forgives great sins, His wonderful grace is clearly displayed.

Fearing the Lord means having a deep, reverent awe that leads to loving obedience. Anyone who respects God in this way will not be left to wander in confusion. God will guide his heart and mind to choose the path of duty that pleases Him.

The person who reveres God enjoys inward peace and rests securely in God's goodness. In ancient times, this blessing included keeping the promised land of Canaan and seeing one's family prosper. God promises enduring security to all who walk closely with Him.

God welcomes those who revere Him into intimate friendship, sharing His heart with them as with trusted companions. He reveals the inner comfort and deep blessings of His covenant to their understanding. While worldly people miss these spiritual truths, humble believers experience God's close presence.

David keeps his eyes fixed on the Lord in constant prayer and expectation. Even when hidden traps and dangers catch his feet, he looks upward to heaven rather than down at the net. He trusts that God alone has the power to pull him free from every snare.

David feels isolated, deserted by friends, and weighed down by sorrow. Because it seems as though God has hidden His face, David begs for a look of loving favor. He offers no claim of personal worth, asking only for undeserved grace in his loneliness.

David's inner grief and anxiety keep growing larger as his outward troubles multiply. His heart feels tightly squeezed and pressed down by pain. He cries out to God as the only deliverer who can rescue him from such overwhelming distress.

David asks God to look upon his painful suffering and hard struggles with deep pity. At the same time, he knows his sins are connected to his distress, so he asks for complete forgiveness. Removing the guilt of sin is his deepest desire, because God's pardon brings true relief.

David asks God to look upon his pursuers, whose numbers are large and whose hostility is cruel. He cannot withstand their violent malice in his own strength. He leaves his foes in God's hands, confident that divine justice will protect him against their hatred.

David prays for the Lord to preserve his life and keep his soul from falling into evil or despair. He reminds God that he has run to Him as a safe shelter. Because he relies on the Lord alone, he trusts that his hope will never end in public shame.

David desires to live with an honest heart and blameless conduct before God and men. As toward his enemies, his conscience is clean, and he prays that doing what is right will guard his life like a shield. He continues to wait patiently for God to defend his cause.

David ends his prayer by interceding for the whole community of God's people. To redeem means to buy back or rescue from danger, and he asks God to free the entire nation from all its troubles. Believers look beyond their own needs to pray for the safety and peace of God's church.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars view this final line as a later liturgical addition for public worship, noting that it falls outside the alphabetical acrostic pattern and uses a different Hebrew name for God.
